en.name: Perilla leaves, fresh
en.summary: Fresh perilla keeps 5–10 days in the fridge at 4 °C (40 °F) or below if the stems stand in water. Unlike basil, perilla does not sulk in the cold, so the fridge is the right place for it.
en.pantry: No room-temperature timeline is published for perilla. A bunch left on the counter in a jar of water will hold for a day or so in a cool kitchen, but the leaves are thin and high in volatile oil, and in Taiwanese summer heat they go limp and lose their scent before the day is out. Treat the counter as a place to park the bunch while you cook, not as storage.
en.fridge: 5–10 days at 4 °C (40 °F) or below — a figure read across from fresh basil rather than measured for perilla. Trim the stem ends, stand them in a small jar with a centimetre of water, drape a bag loosely over the leaves and refrigerate, changing the water every couple of days. Leaves packed flat in a sealed bag are the classic mistake: they bruise against one another and go black at the edges within days. Basil hates the cold and blackens at fridge temperature; perilla does not, which is why the fridge is the right place for it.
en.freezer: No freezer timeline exists for perilla, and freezing whole leaves is not worth it — they thaw to dark, limp tissue with none of the crispness that makes shiso worth wrapping around anything. If you have a glut, the better routes are the ones Taiwanese and Japanese kitchens already use: salt them down, pickle them in soy sauce and sesame oil, or blitz them into a paste with oil, which you can freeze in a flat sheet and break off as needed.
spoilage: Black edges spreading in from the leaf margin.
Limp, translucent patches where leaves were pressed together.
A sour or fermented smell instead of the sharp minty-cumin scent.
Slime on the cut stems or in the water in the jar.
tips: Buy bunches with the stems still on; loose leaves have no way to drink.
Do not wash until you use them — surface water is what blackens the edges.
Keep them away from the coldest back wall of the fridge, where they can freeze and collapse.
A bunch going soft is still fine for pickling in soy sauce even when it is past being pretty.

faq.q: How long do fresh perilla leaves keep?
faq.a: 5–10 days in the fridge at 4 °C (40 °F) or below with the stems in water. Change the water when it clouds.
There is no published freezer timeline, and whole leaves freeze badly — they thaw limp and dark. Salting, soy pickling or making an oil paste all work far better.

faq.q: Should perilla be kept in water like basil?
faq.a: Yes, stems in a little water is the best method, but unlike basil it belongs in the fridge rather than on the counter. Perilla tolerates cold; basil blackens in it.

zh.name: 紫蘇葉
zh.summary: 新鮮紫蘇葉把莖泡在水裡、放 4 °C 以下冷藏，可放 5～10 天。和羅勒不同，紫蘇並不怕冷，所以冰箱就是它該待的地方。
zh.pantry: 紫蘇葉沒有公布的室溫期限。在涼爽的廚房裡，插在水杯裡的一把大概撐得過一天；但葉片薄、揮發性精油又多，台灣夏天的室溫下不到一天就會軟塌、香氣跑光。請把檯面當成做菜時暫放的地方，不要當成保存方式。
zh.fridge: 放 4 °C 以下 5～10 天——這個數字是從新鮮羅勒讀過來的，不是針對紫蘇測出來的。把莖的切口修一下，插進裝著約一公分水的小杯，上面鬆鬆罩一個袋子再放冰箱，水每隔幾天換一次。最常見的錯誤是把葉片平疊著密封進袋子：葉子彼此壓傷，幾天內就從邊緣發黑。羅勒怕冷、在冷藏溫度下會變黑；紫蘇不會，所以冰箱對它來說才是對的地方。
zh.freezer: 紫蘇葉沒有任何冷凍期限可循，而且整片冷凍並不划算——解凍後只剩深色、軟塌的葉片，那股讓人願意拿它包東西的脆爽感完全不見了。量太多的話，走台日廚房本來就在走的路比較實在：抹鹽醃起來、用醬油和麻油漬成醬菜，或加油打成醬泥，把醬泥壓成薄片冷凍，要用再剝一塊。
spoilage: 葉緣開始發黑，並往葉心蔓延。
葉片相疊處出現軟塌、半透明的斑塊。
聞起來發酸或有發酵味，而不是那股帶薄荷與孜然感的香氣。
莖的切口或杯底的水變得黏滑。
tips: 買帶莖的整把，散葉沒有辦法吸水。
要用時才洗；表面的水正是讓葉緣發黑的原因。
不要貼著冰箱最冷的內壁，那裡會把葉片凍傷塌掉。
一把開始變軟、賣相不好的紫蘇，拿去醬油漬還是很好用。

faq.a: 莖插水、放 4 °C 以下冷藏 5～10 天。水一混濁就換掉。
沒有公布的冷凍期限，而且整片冷凍效果很差，解凍後又黑又軟。抹鹽、醬油漬或打成油醬都好得多。

faq.q: 紫蘇葉要像羅勒一樣插水養嗎？
faq.a: 要，莖插一點水是最好的方法，但和羅勒不同，它該放冰箱而不是室溫。紫蘇耐冷，羅勒一冷就發黑。
